analysis.one_liner: Lets the Labor Department fine insurers and employers who shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a bipartisan introduction in May 2023, it sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires health plans to cover mental health and substance use treatment on par with physical health care. But the Department of Labor currently has no power to fine plans that violate that rule, so violations often go unpunished. This bill would create civil monetary penalties for plan sponsors, administrators, and insurers that fail to meet the parity requirement, and let the Department of Labor enforce it directly.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer health insurance who need mental health or substance use treatment. With fines on the table, plans and insurers would have a financial reason to cover therapy, inpatient care, and addiction treatment at the same level as physical care, instead of restricting them in ways the current law forbids.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA to add civil monetary penalties for any plan sponsor, plan administrator, or issuer that fails to meet the mental health and substance use disorder parity requirements, and gives the Department of Labor authority to enforce them directly.

Currently the Department of Labor lacks a penalty tool for parity violations; adding fines gives the agency leverage to make plans comply rather than relying on lawsuit-by-lawsuit enforcement by individuals.
The penalties would apply to plan years starting at least one year after enactment, giving plans time to bring their mental health coverage into compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor group health plans and insurers that administer them, who would face civil fines for parity violations and would have to pay for the mental health and substance use benefits they were already legally required to cover.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs fall partly on employers, including small ones, who fund group health plans; fines and required coverage upgrades could raise premium costs, and some of that cost can be passed to workers through premiums or wages.

The bill relies on Labor Department enforcement activity; the amount of the penalties and how aggressively they are pursued would depend on the administration in power, so the practical benefit could vary from one administration to the next.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core requirement — covering mental health care on par with physical care — has been federal law since 2008; this bill only adds teeth to enforce it. The main cost is on employers and insurers to bring coverage into compliance with rules they already follow on paper. The tradeoff is modest: real enforcement against a small share of violators in exchange for access to mental health and addiction treatment that many people are currently denied.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Donald Norcross introduced the bill on May 30, 2023, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The bill attracted 11 cosponsors, 10 Democrats and 1 Republican, but no further action was ever taken on it.
No committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers that would have faced fines for violating mental health parity rules are better off; the enforcement never happened, and people denied mental health coverage gained nothing.

for.name: Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add Labor Department fines for mental health parity violations.

for.name: Original cosponsors: Joe Courtney, Brian Fitzpatrick, Ann Kuster, David Trone, Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no additional members joined after introduction.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 30, 2023 and never scheduled it for consideration; it never advanced past the committee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 10 of 11 cosponsors were Democrats, with Republican Brian Fitzpatrick the lone GOP supporter, and the bill never advanced to a vote where a full partisan split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let the Labor Department fine insurers who administer group plans that fail to cover mental health care on par with physical care. Their gain from the status quo is avoided coverage costs that the law already says they must bear.

Plan sponsors and administrators would be directly liable for civil fines under the bill. Most large employers already provide some mental health coverage, so the cost lands mainly on those whose plans fall short.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Enforced parity means fewer denials and restrictions on therapy, inpatient care, and substance use treatment, which would increase demand for these services and access for patients.
